h1-emuA.text:
One thing that comes to mind is that you have someone, ie your peers, to reality check with any downloads. While great insight can come from psychedelics so too can a lot of bullshit, and often they feel exactly the same in the bright shining light. Having a few friends who know you pretty well can be helpful in seeing what is insightful vs. just stuff you already knew, or is about your mom.

It gives you a community, and in some traditional medicines it makes it so you only do ceremonies when the group does ceremonies. This can help with compulsive use and integration.

It can also help to have people to do things like watch the kids that you trust, not have to drive, have people to get you water, sit with you until your conscious again, etc.

h1-emuB.text:
Your peers can help you reality check any downloads you got from the experience. Psychedelics can give you insight but they can also give you nonsense and make it seem equally valid because everything is covered in a bright shining light. A few friends who know your history can help you suss out what parts are insight and what parts are just...mom.

It sounds cheesy but a community can help ground your ceremonies in a schedule. Many traditional medicines only allow ceremonies at specific times for the whole group. This schedule can help you avoid compulsive overuse and give you time to integrate.

It's nice to have a community to help you organize logistics like trusted child care, not having to drive, or having people to help you with simple things like water when you're coming down.

h2-emuA.text: One other aspect of working in community that is very helpful, is the ability to set up ceremony times that work for the entire group. Many traditional medical systems do this. It helps to prevent compulsive over-use of medicine and allows for appropriate integration time between ceremonies.

h2-emuB.text: One of the benefits of community is that many traditional medicinal practices occur within ceremonies that have a schedule. The schedule of ceremonies, rather than people doing ceremonies when they want, serves to limit compulsive use and provide for integration time.

h3-emuA.text:
Mine was the first one I did, and I don’t work with special shamans. I know this goes against most traditional lineages. With ayahuasca and Bwiti in particular there is a strong belief among most groups that the medicine should only be taken by people within the lineage and under the authority of those people.

I oppose this for a number of reasons but primarily because putting one charismatic individual above everyone else is a terrible idea. Especially when you have people flying around the world leading retreats, how do you know that your charismatic individual is actually a good person? He or she could be unvetted, unaccountable, a sexual predator, financially dependent on you needing to keep coming back to him, or just plain wrong. The deeper you go the more it matters.

h3-emuB.text:
First one is that there is no such thing as a shaman. I know this goes against what most traditional lineages would tell you. Most ayahuasca lineages, most Bwiti traditions, etc., will tell you that the medicine is only to be taken under the authority of someone trained in their lineage.

My problem is that it puts a charismatic individual on a pedestal where they shouldn’t be. When someone is holding themselves out as the person who will lead you through your experience as part of a retreat, they may or may not be who they say they are. They may be unvetted, unaccountable, sexual predators, financially dependent on your continued business, or just plain wrong. And when you’re opening up, those are important things to know.

h5-emuA.text:
There are other medicines and protocols that I consider more destabilizing and more of a medical burden (like some ketamine, mmda, bufo protocols. See those articles.

The use of this medicine is secondary to all of the other pl/ork you should be doing to increase your capacity for reparenting, somatic capacity, and peer counseling, etc. The medicine will enhance that. It will not replace months of those other kinds of relationships in any kind of pharmacological short cut.

Bonus: by setting up a pre-req, you weed out people who are just looking to collect experiences. If they are not willing to commit to 6 months of learning to be a good listener, they are not likely to be relationally matured by the visions they might get here.

Integration is your life. If the ceremonies did anything at all, they will show up in your life after you leave. How are you relating? How are you acting? How are you sleeping? Making decisions? Handling frustration?

h5-emuB.text:
Note: For certain medicines and protocols that I perceive as more destabilizing or more of a medical burden (some ketamine, mdma, and bufo protocols, for example), I would be even more concerned with whether these prerequisites were met. See those articles for why.

The medicine is always secondary to the other pl/ork. Reparenting/somatic work and peer counseling can always be done, and the medicine can be a useful tool to enhance that work. But no medicine is going to replace those things, pharmacologically.

There is another benefit to this pre-req – it weeds out those who only want to collect experiences. If they are unwilling to make a 6 month commitment to learning how to counsel their peers, it is unlikely they will come out of a ceremony having gained a lot of relational maturity, regardless of how mindblowing the geometric shapes they saw were.

Integration is your life. If the ceremony has any effect on you at all, it will come out in your life after you leave the ceremony. Your relationships, your day to day behavior, your sleep habits, your decision making, your ability to tolerate frustration, etc.

h6-emuA.text:
The medicine is behind the other pl/ork in terms of priority. Reparenting, somatic capacity and peer counselling need to be done first. The medicine will enhance something you are already doing. The medicine cannot replace months of relationship work through pharmacology.

As a bonus, it forces you to do that pre-req work so you aren’t just some experience collector. If you aren’t willing to do 6 months of relationship work before doing the medicine then it is unlikely the medicine is going to magically make you relationally mature because the visions were interestingly geometric.

h6-emuB.text:
I would keep medicine behind a bit of a wall of other pl/ork. Reparenting, working on somatic capacity, peer counseling work, etc. Some people do come in with this work under their belt and it’s amazing to deep dive with them, but I’ve rarely seen it be a good idea to start with medicine, as it can’t really pharmacologically create the relational capacity that other things can over time.

This also comes with the benefit of filtering out experience collectors - if you aren’t willing to do at least 6 months of work on something like listening skills I’m highly skeptical that you’ll be any more relationally mature post experience.
